President Trump said Monday, after weeks of criticism from both parties, that taxpayers will no longer pay for the TV ads promoting him and his administration, and that he and his super PAC will cover the cost going forward.
Getting into it: In a Truth Social post, Trump defended the ads as “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” but said he and MAGA Inc., his super PAC with more than $400 million on hand, would pay for them instead. A White House official clarified that the PAC will only fund ads moving forward and won’t repay the government for spots that already aired, which ad-tracking firm AdImpact estimates cost about $10 million.
The ads, which ended with the line “Paid for by the U.S. Government,” ran during football games and shows like “Saturday Night Live,” and one was nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad. The New York Times reported last week that the order to pay for the ads with public money came straight from Trump to his budget director, and that on Sept. 19 the budget office moved $20 million out of Customs and Border Protection’s funds into a new line labeled “One Big Beautiful Bill Commemorative Events” to cover them.
The reversal came hours after Vice President JD Vance defended the ads, comparing them to the Obama administration’s Affordable Care Act campaign and saying, “I don’t think there’s anything unusual or unorthodox about it.” But critics from both parties had called the spending improper, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who said the ads “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” and Sen. Thom Tillis, who compared Trump to Hungary’s Viktor Orbán. Sen. Maggie Hassan, who first demanded answers from the White House, said the ads “were clearly wrong and clearly illegal” and that Trump “should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent.”
This all comes as California Attorney General Rob Bonta called for an outside probe Monday into what he called a “staggering misuse of public funding.” The watchdog group Public Citizen has also asked federal investigators to look into whether the ads broke laws against government propaganda, though FCC Chair Brendan Carr said last week he had no problem with the ads and turned down a request to review them.

sources.news_title: Trump yields after backlash on taxpayer-funded ‘God Made Trump’ ad
sources.text:
The Freedom From Religion Foundation welcomes President Trump’s reversal of plans to use taxpayer dollars to pay for campaign-style advertisements promoting himself. However, this doesn’t excuse his administration for putting public funds toward the effort in the first place.
After mounting criticism, Trump has announced that his super PAC, MAGA Inc., rather than American taxpayers, will pay for the commercials. The U-turn comes after more than $10 million worth of taxpayer-funded ads have already aired since September, according to AdImpact. The advertisements were funded through a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract using public money.
“If Trump and his political supporters want to spend their own money glorifying him, that is their business,” say FFRF Co-Presidents Dan Barker and Annie Laurie Gaylor. “American taxpayers should never have been forced to bankroll this self-serving propaganda. We’re pleased that public pressure forced the president to back down.”
The administration’s plans were especially alarming because among the campaign-style advertisements produced for the effort was a three-minute “God Made Trump” video portraying the president as a divinely chosen leader. The ad, originally created by the pro-Trump Dilley Meme Team, is a risible riff on Paul Harvey’s famous “So God Made a Farmer” speech. It repeatedly, and ludicrously, suggests that Trump was personally created and selected by God for his political role. “I need somebody … to remain strong in faith and know the belief in God and country,” the narrator intones among many other claims, repeatedly concluding: “So God made Trump.”
FFRF strongly objected to the prospect of the federal government using taxpayer money to disseminate such overtly religious political propaganda. The federal government has no business using public resources to elevate the president politically while wrapping him in a mantle of divine authority.
The White House initially defended the advertisements as public service announcements. Trump himself defended using taxpayer money for them just days before reversing course, telling reporters: “I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”
But, thankfully, Trump has changed course. “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA Inc.,” Trump announced.
FFRF says the reversal is welcome, but it does not erase the serious questions raised by the administration’s original decision or the millions of public dollars reportedly already spent.
“The fact that Trump backed down demonstrates why speaking out against abuses of government power matters,” Gaylor and Barker add. “Taxpayer money belongs to the American people. It is not a political slush fund for presidents to advertise themselves, and it certainly must not be used to promote the notion that our political leaders have been chosen by God.”
FFRF has made repeated warnings concerning the efforts of Trump and his allies to portray his political career as part of a divine plan, including Trump’s claim that God spared him from assassination so that he could return to the presidency. Such rhetoric is a hallmark of Christian nationalism, which seeks to fuse religious identity with political power and portray political leaders and objectives as divinely ordained.
Trump’s turnabout is a welcome development. But American taxpayers never should have had to foot the bill for disinformation.
The Freedom From Religion Foundation is a U.S.-based nonprofit dedicated to defending the constitutional principle of separation between state and church and educating the public on matters relating to nontheism. With approximately 40,000 members, FFRF is the largest association of freethinkers (atheists, agnostics and humanists) in North America. For more information, visit ffrf.org.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump is playing damage control after being caught red-handed misusing taxpayer dollars for a desperate election-year advertising campaign.
On Monday, Trump suddenly announced the government’s role in his propagandistic TV ad campaign, which had reportedly been illegally using taxpayer funds that Congress appropriated to the Department of Homeland Security.
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money. This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Of course, the ads were not promoting the United States. They were promoting Trump, the Republican Party, and the party’s election-year messaging about a purported rise in communism and socialism.
Announcing that the ads would now be run by MAGA Inc., Trump’s super PAC, is a tacit admission of what was clear all along: These were partisan election ads. According to reports, Trump had explicitly requested that taxpayer funds be used in the pro-Trump, pro-GOP ad campaign.
Trump’s retreat also undermines his team’s excuses for wasting tax dollars.
Just hours before Trump’s reversal, Vice President JD Vance was falsely comparing the ads to public service ads run by past presidents like Barack Obama.
“If you look historically—go back to the Obama administration with the Affordable Care Act, you have the people’s government using tax dollars to advertise about what the government is doing,” Vance said.
Of course, an ad advising people to sign up for health insurance is not remotely the same as one effectively telling people to vote Republican.
Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff of California responded to Trump’s announcement, writing on Bluesky, “You spoke out, and he backed down.”
“Now let’s see the proof this illegal waste of your taxes is over for good. And that he pays the money back. We don’t want the U.S. taxpayers to be the latest contractors to get stiffed,” Schiff added.
Democrats have launched investigations into which government resources and personnel were used for the creation and distribution of the ads. They have said that the ads violated laws against use of public resources for partisan activity, such as the Hatch Act, as well as laws against the creation of propaganda.
The entire episode underlines the dire straits Republicans find themselves in the month before Election Day. Trump and his party continue to fall in popularity or their electoral chances, with voters indicating their enthusiasm to flip Congress’ control to the Democrats.
Instead of reversing course, Trump’s first instinct—as it so often is—was to break the law.

sources.news_title: Trump Ends Taxpayer Funding for Promotional TV Ads, Says He or MAGA Inc. Will Cover Costs
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said taxpayer money will no longer be used for a series of nationally broadcast television advertisements promoting his administration, announcing that future costs will instead be covered personally or through MAGA Inc. after bipartisan criticism of the government-funded campaign.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
President Donald Trump said Monday that taxpayers will no longer finance a series of television advertisements featuring him and promoting his administration, reversing course after lawmakers and ethics experts from both parties questioned whether federal money was being used for political messaging weeks before the November congressional elections.
Trump defended the advertisements but said he would shift the cost away from the government and instead pay personally or use money raised through MAGA Inc., the super PAC aligned with him.
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
“This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” Trump added.
The decision followed mounting scrutiny over three advertisements that aired nationally, including during high-profile professional and college football broadcasts. The spots carried disclaimers indicating they were paid for by the U.S. government.
At least $11 million had already been spent airing the advertisements, according to Associated Press reporting. Democratic lawmakers have said the administration transferred $20 million in Department of Homeland Security funding for the broader advertising effort.
One advertisement features Trump declaring that “America will never be a communist country,” accompanied by a chorus repeating “love me.” Another pairs images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump describing what he calls a “golden age of America.”
A separate ad incorporated language and imagery resembling material used during Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, further fueling questions about whether a government-funded public-service campaign had crossed into political promotion.
The administration had drawn the funding from money provided to the Department of Homeland Security under a previous reconciliation law, according to congressional and media reports. An apportionment document showed $20 million transferred into an account designated for commemorative events, with money subsequently used for the advertisements.
Criticism came from both sides of the aisle.
Democratic Sens. Patty Murray of Washington and Chris Murphy of Connecticut called the spending an “illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars” in a letter challenging the advertising campaign. They also pointed to existing restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for publicity or propaganda.
Republican lawmakers also raised concerns. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sens. John Kennedy and Thom Tillis were among Republicans publicly questioning whether taxpayer money should finance advertisements centered heavily on the president shortly before an election.
The White House had defended the spots as public-service messages highlighting administration policies rather than campaign advertisements. Trump similarly argued that the content promoted the United States rather than his own electoral interests.
Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, declined a request to investigate the advertisements and said he considered them permissible.
Other officials and watchdog groups disagreed. Democratic Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California requested independent investigations, while the advocacy organization Public Citizen filed a complaint questioning the legality of the campaign.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta separately called for an independent investigation Monday, describing the use of government funding for the advertisements as a misuse of public money.
The controversy also prompted questions under federal restrictions governing government propaganda and political activity.
Federal appropriations laws have long prohibited agencies from using taxpayer funds for certain forms of “publicity or propaganda” not specifically authorized by Congress. The Hatch Act separately restricts partisan political activity by many federal employees, although its application depends on who participated, what actions were taken and whether the communication constituted prohibited political activity.
Trump’s announcement avoids further taxpayer financing of the advertisements but does not by itself resolve whether money already spent will be reimbursed to the government.
It was not immediately clear Monday whether MAGA Inc. or Trump personally would repay the Treasury for previous expenditures or simply assume the costs of advertisements going forward.
MAGA Inc. has substantial financial resources available. The super PAC had accumulated more than $400 million by late summer, giving it ample capacity to purchase television advertising independently of the federal government.
The dispute has attracted heightened attention because the advertisements began airing shortly before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, even though Trump himself is not on the ballot.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey released Tuesday found broad public opposition to using taxpayer funds for election-related television advertising featuring Trump or members of his administration. Eighty-six percent of respondents opposed such spending, including 80% of Republicans surveyed.
The advertising campaign had reached viewers across multiple networks and markets, including broadcasts on major television outlets and during sporting events with large national audiences.
Administration officials maintained that the commercials were intended to promote government achievements and patriotic themes rather than solicit votes. Critics countered that their timing, presentation and similarities to campaign advertising made the distinction difficult to sustain.
Trump’s decision now shifts that debate.
Rather than continuing to defend taxpayer financing of the spots, the president has chosen to move future expenditures to private political funds or his own money while continuing to stand behind the substance of the advertisements.
The change eliminates the most immediate dispute over who will pay for future broadcasts, but questions remain over how the original federal funds were authorized, whether existing appropriations restrictions were followed and whether any of the taxpayer money already spent will ultimately be returned.

sources.text:
President Trump has reversed course and ordered the government to stop paying for his campaign-style ads that Uncle Sam had been bankrolling with millions in taxpayer dollars.
In a rare retreat, Trump said he would instruct the MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward to pay to air the provocative ads, which are virtually identical to ones his campaign funded during his 2024 presidential run.
“I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” Trump wrote on his social media site.
Democrats Tuesday cheered the unusual Trump flip-flop, which they said was likely due to a backlash from voters and pushback from endangered Republican lawmakers.
“It’s never because he wants to, but I’m glad he was pushed into making right decision,” said Rep. Joe Morelle (D-New York), who leads a Democratic effort to counter what it calls Trump efforts to improperly meddle in the midterms.
Critics have said they will push the White House to repay the government for the more than $20 million spent so far and pledge to avoid spending any more public money on the spots.
Trump did not mention any plan to reimburse the feds for the money it has spent on the questionable ads so far, which were funded by the Department of Homeland Security, whose mission is supposed to be to keep Americans safe from terrorism and other threats.
With the midterm congressional elections looming in just a month’s time, Trump ordered the use of millions in federal funds to air at least three ads, mostly during weekend pro and college football games.
One 30-second black-and-white spot depicts the president grimly striding down a hallway as he calls for a “final battle” against “globalists” and the “fake news media.”
“We will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” he intones in the ad.
It ends with Trump staring straight into the camera lens as a message appears saying: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.” The exact same ad aired during the 2024 campaign, except that it had a standard tag that it was paid for by his presidential campaign.
Trump and other White House officials defended the ads as a “reminder to Americans to love their country.” Vice President JD Vance defended Trump’s decision to order taxpayer funding for the partisan message, just hours before Trump pulled the plug on it.
Even as he reversed course, Trump repeated his defense of the ads as inoffensive public service messages. Some officials compared them to previous administrations’ paying for ads to urge Americans to take advantage of government benefits, like the Affordable Care Act, Medicare or COVID vaccinations.
“I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money. This is a rather standard thing to do,” Trump wrote on his social media site.
Even Trump’s new plan may be legally dubious, critics say.
Super PACs like MAGA Inc. are legally required to make spending decisions independently and not coordinate with political candidates, a rule Trump appears to be openly violating by vowing to instruct MAGA Inc. to pay for the ads.

BS BULLETIN:
- Trump says the government will stop footing the bill for his controversial “patriotic” television ads.
- The president still insists using taxpayer money for them was perfectly legitimate.

President Trump has apparently discovered one way to end the argument over who should pay for his “patriotic” television commercials.
Not you.
After days of defending the use of taxpayer money for ads featuring himself and his administration, Trump announced Monday that he would change course and use political money instead.
Trump wrote:
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money.”
He then defended the practice:
“This is a rather standard thing to do.”
But despite maintaining that there was nothing improper about it, Trump announced the switch:
“I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
That last clause is important.
Trump said “pay for them myself,” but the White House confirmed that MAGA Inc., the super PAC supporting him, will finance the ads going forward.
The controversy began after government-funded commercials featuring Trump started appearing on television with the disclaimer:
“Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
One of the ads echoed Trump’s 2024 campaign rhetoric, including warnings about communism, socialism and Marxism. Another featured Trump promising to fight the “deep state,” “globalists,” “communists” and the “fake news media.”
The White House defended the spots as public-service announcements intended to promote the country and administration policies rather than election advertising.
Critics weren’t buying it.
And unusually for Washington these days, objections didn’t come exclusively from Democrats.
Republicans including Sens. John Thune, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis publicly questioned whether taxpayer money should be paying for advertisements that looked an awful lot like political campaign material.
The administration had already spent at least $1.5 million in federal money on the ads, according to Associated Press reporting. Other reporting has described a broader government media campaign worth considerably more.
Trump had vigorously defended the spending just days earlier.
Asked about the commercials last week, he argued that they weren’t campaign advertising because he isn’t on the ballot.
“I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office.”
He said the advertisements were instead:
“for the spirit of our country.”
Now that spirit will apparently have a new billing address.
One unresolved question is what happens to the taxpayer money already spent.
The administration’s announcement concerns how the ads will be financed going forward, and available reporting does not establish that MAGA Inc. will reimburse the Treasury for the federal money already used.
MY QUICK TAKE
There is actually a wonderfully old-fashioned solution buried in all of this.
If a politician wants to run an advertisement telling America how terrific his administration is, political donors can pay for it.
Remarkable concept.
What makes Trump’s reversal entertaining is that he isn’t conceding the critics were right. His position is essentially: I was allowed to make you pay for these — but since you’re going to complain about it, fine, I’ll find somebody else.
And “I’ll pay for them myself” immediately followed by “with money I raised for MAGA Inc.” may be one of the most Washington definitions of myself we’ve encountered in quite some time.
The bigger point is that criticism from his own side mattered here. When Democrats complain about Trump, everybody knows the choreography. When John Thune, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis start asking why taxpayers are underwriting campaign-looking television spots, somebody in the room begins checking the invoice.
This time, apparently, they found a different credit card.

Facing backlash, Trump says his super PAC will pay for taxpayer-funded ads
President Donald Trump reversed course Monday and announced that his super political action committee would now pay for the television ads promoting him that have been airing nationwide at taxpayer expense.
In a post on his social media platform, Trump wrote, “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
More than $10 million in taxpayer-funded ads have run since September, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking service. The ads, which are running on cable and network television, were paid for through a $20 million contract that used funds from the Department of Homeland Security.
Democrats — and some Republicans — have criticized the ads as a possible violation of federal laws for using taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes.” The ads were broadcast in the heat of the campaign for the midterms, as Republicans are trying to hold control of Congress. At least one of the ads featured footage that originally had appeared in a 2024 Trump campaign video.
The White House had defended the ads as simply public service announcements. But the use of material that had originated in a campaign provided further fuel to critics of the ads.
There were four different ads, and each featured an unusual disclaimer: “Paid for by the U.S. government.”
One of them featured images of Trump as the song “Love Me” by Christian Berishaj played. The artist, who performs as JMSN, has complained about the use of his song.
The New York Times wrote over the weekend that Trump had personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads. Federal records show that U.S. Customs and Border Protection, which falls under the Department of Homeland Security, awarded a contract to LMD, a Maryland marketing firm, on Sept. 20.
Trump referred to the backlash in his post.
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” he wrote, defending them as “a rather standard thing to do.”
The White House did not immediately respond to an email for comment or how the president’s super PAC would pay for the ads. A spokesperson for MAGA Inc. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump has rarely acknowledged bowing to popular pressure in his second term.
Trump’s claim in his social media post that he would pay for the ads “myself” through his super PAC is likely to add fodder to another formal complaint against the president.
A campaign watchdog, the Campaign Legal Center, accused Trump of violating federal election laws by directing his super PAC in a complaint to the Federal Election Commission because of his previous claims to control the super PAC.
Trump has referred to the super PAC’s funds as “my money that I control” in the past.
Federal law bars federal officeholders from directing spending decisions for a political organization with no contribution limits, such as a super PAC.
Alex Pfeiffer, a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., said at the time, “MAGA Inc. fully complies with the law.”
Trump’s political committee can certainly afford to pay for the ads: MAGA Inc. entered September with about $415 million on hand. MAGA Inc. and two super PACs affiliated with it have since set aside about $194 million for advertising ahead of November, according to AdImpact data.
Trump had defended the use of taxpayer money for the spots just five days earlier. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, the president said: “If somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money.”
“But these are ads for the country,” he said. “You have to understand. I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

California Attorney General Rob Bonta also called for investigations on Monday, alleging that the spending constituted a misuse of public funds.

President Donald Trump has announced he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television advertisements promoting his policies and personal message.
What Happened
Trump made the announcement on social media, citing a ‘bipartisan pushback’ against the use of government money for political ads.
He said the ads, which highlight his tax cuts, manufacturing policies, and opposition to the ‘deep state,’ were ‘a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.’

Background: How Government Ads Work
Under US law, public funds may not be used to promote a specific political candidate or policy.
Historically, government ads have focused on public health or emergencies—such as vaccine outreach or disaster preparedness.
Trump’s ads, however, promote his personal leadership and policies, raising concerns about the purpose of the spending.

There is no clear legal precedent for ads that promote a president’s policies without a public service function.
While the ads were not officially sanctioned by the executive branch, their funding source—stated as ‘U.S. Government’—raises compliance questions.
Legal experts like Margaret Dylus-Yukins say it’s difficult to justify spending public funds on ads with only a political purpose.

"Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," the official said.

"They're not partisan. They're not -- you know, it's not like we're advocating for a particular candidate. We're trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is," Vance said.
Trump defended the ads last week at an event in the Oval Office, saying they were "for the spirit of our country" and not a political endorsement for Republican candidates on the ballot this November or for his administration's policies.
"You have to understand; I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office. I'm promoting the country," Trump said.
"Now, if somebody said that that's wrong, I'll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country," he said.
Trump has implored Republican voters to "pretend" that he is on the ballot in the November midterm elections to boost voter turnout for GOP congressional candidates.
The federal government has spent at least $2.5 million to air the TV ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an advertising agency that analyzes ad spending across television.
A total of $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security's budget had been allocated for the effort.
Ethics watchdogs and several Congressional Democrats -- as well as some Republicans -- have said the ads are inappropriate. Some critics have said the ads could violate federal propaganda law.
Four ads have been aired over the last two weeks. One features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing "the final battle" against "the deep state," "the globalists," and "the sick political class that hates our country."
Another ad includes a montage of clips and images of Trump at events and rallies featuring onscreen text about the "largest tax cuts in history."
The latest ad, released last week, focuses on the U.S. war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Audio of Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage, including unclassified strikes, is displayed.
The video in the ad appears to be the same as one played during the Republican midterm convention last month. And it played last Wednesday before Hegseth addressed 600 service members in his State of the Force speech at the Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia.

sources.news_title: Trump says his super PAC will pay for taxpayer-funded ads that sparked backlash for glorifying him - Now Georgia
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday that he will stop using taxpayer funds for television advertisements glorifying himself that sparked a major backlash, and instead tap his super PAC to cover costs going forward.
In a post on his social media site, Trump defended the ads, which cost at least $1.5 million in federal funds and have drawn intense criticism. Trump said they were “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.”
“This is a rather standard thing to do,” the president wrote, while blaming intense criticism for using taxpayer funds on the ads on the “Radical Left.” But the president added that he’d “decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
That is Trump’s political war chest, which had amassed more than $400 million by the end of July. Trump has begun to tap it to boost Republican candidates around the country ahead of midterm elections.
Trump provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such future advertising.
The White House — which had fiercely defended using taxpayer money on spots meant to promote the president — said Monday night that MAGA Inc. will pay for such ads going forward. It did not answer questions on how it or Trump might prove that his political funds were being used on such future advertising.
Trump’s abrupt about-face came after leaders from both parties criticized using taxpayer funds for the ads.
Legal experts said the ads might even violate federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for “publicity or propaganda” and one limiting the partisan political activities of government employees.
The spots began airing in late September
The first ad featured clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history,” “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police.”
Later the same week, a second ad began running. It showed scenic videos of Mount Rushmore with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary.
A third, more recent one was virtually identical to an ad for Trump’s Republican reelection campaign in 2024 and showed him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.”
All ended with a message: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
According to AdImpact, which tracks media spending, the spots had cost at least $1.4 million by the end of September. The actual amount spent could be far more, depending on whether networks classified the ad as a political ad.
